newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran assembly debates moderate president's cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Iran assembly debates moderate president's cabinet.

text.p: Iran's parliament on Tuesday began debate on the cabinet nominees of President Mohammad Khatami, who urged it to approve all his ministers and said Iran needed a "fresh presence" in foreign relations.
The 11 deputies who spoke in the first five-hour session were backers of the moderate Khatami, who was in parliament to show support for his 22 proposed ministers.
Parliament was to reconvene later on Tuesday for another session during which conservative deputies were expected to criticise some nominees.

"In foreign relations we need an active and fresh presence based on our independence and national interests," Khatami told parliament. "It is important for us to defuse tensions and seek friendship and brotherhood in the international arena."
"We have to exploit all possibilities to promote and progress our country in the world based upon the three principles of dignity, wisdom and expediency," Khatami said.

Iran has no ties with the United States, which has imposed sanctions on Tehran, and its relations with Europe are tense. It has worked over the past year towards improving fragile ties with its Gulf Arab neighbours.
Analysts do not expect Khatami, sworn in this month after a May landslide election victory, to herald major changes in foreign policy, the domain of supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Khatami asked the parliament, or Majlis, to give its vote of confidence to all ministers so that "the stagnation we are witnessing will come to an end as soon as possible".
The parliament was expected to vote on Wednesday after a five-hour session dedicated to the cabinet nominees, who would defend themselves and their programmes.

"In the elections, people called for fundamental changes in the management of the country so as a deputy I feel obliged to respect the people's vote and agree with the proposed cabinet of the elected president," said deputy Lotfollah Zarei Qanavati.
"The people gave us an ultimatum with their vote in the presidential election and are now watching us closely," said deputy Hassan Dehgan.

Analysts said some comments by deputies appeared to be a thinly veiled warning to conservatives that it was politically unwise to vote against ministers proposed by a president who enjoyed wide support.
Khatami, a moderate 54-year-old Shi'ite Moslem cleric, was expected to lose at least one of his nominees at the hands of conservatives and radicals in parliament, analysts had said.
Khatami told the 270-seat parliament his programme was based on reinforcing the rule of law and increasing popular participation in politics and other areas of life.

"We have had many crises in the past years. Now it's the era of consolidating and stabilising the Islamic Republic," he said. "This requires a powerful state but the basis of a powerful state is proper relations with the people so that the system should be based on law."
Khatami was swept to power after scooping the votes of the youth, women and the middle class who saw him as a leader able to inject social and economic freedoms into their country.

Despite the expected loss of at least one minister in a sensitive domestic portfolio, Khatami would still emerge with the majority of his cabinet largely intact and his election mandate for change undamaged, the analysts said.

Opposition was expected from conservatives to the proposed minister of culture, Ataollah Mohajerani -- a controversial figure for his support in 1990 of a resumption of talks with Washington -- and interior minister Abdollah Nouri.

"The ministry of culture needs a cultural expert who can be a harbour and refuge for authors, artists and intellectuals. Mohajerani is such a person," deputy Gholamheidar Ibrahim Baysalami said during the debate.

The Culture Ministry has emerged as a battleground between Khatami's supporters, who want to breathe more freedoms into the country, and conservatives who see the ministry as the main weapon against a "Western cultural invasion".
The ministry has power over what media, books, films and music are allowed in the country.
